Mississippi.notes: Source: Form 80-100-25-1-1-000 (Rev. 12/25), 2025 resident instructions. Tax rates: 'Income Tax: 0% on the first $10,000.00 of taxable income and 4.4% on taxable income in excess of $10,000.00.' Single: exemption $6,000 (deduction, not a credit) and standard deduction $2,300, neither phased. Mississippi computes its own gross income (Form 80-105/80-107), not federal AGI. No deduction for federal income tax. No low-income credit for single filers. Same values at $20k/$40k/$80k/$120k. Example: at $40k wages, taxable = 40,000 - 2,300 - 6,000 = 31,700, and tax = 4.4% x 21,700 = $954.80. Matches Tax Foundation exactly. Later law: HB 1 (2025, eff. July 1, 2025) cuts the rate on income over $10,000 to 4.0% in 2026, then 3.75%/3.5%/3.25% for 2027-2029 and 3% from 2030, with possible further cuts. The 2025 rate is unchanged. Mississippi did not adopt the federal tips/overtime deductions; it does not start from federal income. No local income taxes. Structure label: Mississippi's 2025 tax is often described as a flat 4.4% rate with a $10,000 zero-rate band (Tax Foundation lists it among flat-tax states); it is coded 'graduated' with an explicit 0% bracket so that bracket-iterating code is used.
Mississippi.changes_vs_2024: Rate on taxable income over $10,000 fell from 4.7% (2024, per 2024 Form 80-100 instructions) to 4.4% (2025), as scheduled by HB 531 (2022). The $10,000 zero bracket, $2,300 standard deduction and $6,000 exemption are unchanged. Effect: 0.3 points on taxable income above $10,000, e.g. about $65 less at $40k wages ($31,700 taxable: $954.80 vs $1,019.90).

Missouri.notes: Official 2025 Tax Chart: $0-$1,313, $0; over $1,313, 2.0% of the excess; over $2,626, $26 + 2.5%; over $3,939, $59 + 3.0%; over $5,252, $98 + 3.5%; over $6,565, $144 + 4.0%; over $7,878, $197 + 4.5%; over $9,191, $256 + 4.7% of the excess. The chart's dollar bases are rounded; the exact cumulative amounts from the brackets differ by under $1. The 2025 MO-1040 line 14 standard deduction for single/MFS is $15,750, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) federal amount, not $15,000. Computation: federal AGI (line 1) plus or minus MO-A modifications gives Missouri AGI (lines 5 and 6). Then subtract the federal income tax deduction (line 13: federal tax x the AGI-based percentage, capped at $5,000 for single; see federal_tax_deduction) and the $15,750 standard deduction to get Missouri taxable income, then apply the tax chart. Missouri has no personal exemption for a single filer. The federal tax deduction depends on actual federal liability. Federal changes such as the tips, overtime, and senior deductions affect Missouri only indirectly, through lower federal tax and so a smaller deduction. The MO-1040 instructions list no Missouri subtraction for tips or overtime, and federal AGI excludes those below-the-line deductions. Illustrative 2025 values, computed with 2025 federal single brackets ($11,925/$48,475/$103,350) and the $15,750 federal standard deduction (not an official worksheet): $20k wages: federal tax $425, deduction 35% = $149, MO TI $4,101, tax about $64. $40k: federal tax $2,671.50, deduction 25% = $668, MO TI $23,582, tax about $932 (about $964 without the deduction). $80k: federal tax $9,049, deduction 15% = $1,357, MO TI $62,893, tax about $2,780. $120k: federal tax $17,867, deduction 5% = $893, MO TI $103,357, tax about $4,682. Credits not included: the Missouri Working Family Tax Credit (20% of the federal EIC as of 1/1/2021 law, needs federal EIC eligibility and tax liability). Local: Kansas City and the City of St. Louis levy 1% earnings taxes on residents (all earnings) and on nonresidents for work done in the city (kcmo.gov; stlouis-mo.gov Collector of Revenue). typical_local_income_tax_rate uses the Tax Foundation footnote (a) statewide average of 0.21% of AGI (2022 data). Use 0.01 for a worker or resident in KC or St. Louis City. Tax Foundation discrepancy: TF lists a $15,000 standard deduction (the pre-OBBBA 2025 federal figure); the official 2025 MO-1040 uses $15,750. Brackets and rates match TF.

federal_tax_deduction.base: Federal tax from MO-1040 line 11: federal Form 1040 line 22 minus lines 27a (EIC) and 29, plus specified Schedule 2/3 items (line 9), plus 'other federal tax' (line 10). Federal income tax withheld is not used.
federal_tax_deduction.agi_definition: Missouri adjusted gross income (MO-1040 line 6). agi_max is inclusive: '$25,000 or less', '$25,001 to $50,000', and so on; $125,001 or more is 0%.

Missouri.changes_vs_2024: Top rate fell from 4.8% to 4.7%. The brackets were indexed: 2024 was 0% to $1,273, then 2.0%-4.5% steps of $1,273, and 4.8% over $8,911 ($248 base); 2025 is 0% to $1,313, $1,313 steps, and 4.7% over $9,191 ($256 base). The single standard deduction rose from $14,600 to $15,750, following the federal amount as raised by P.L. 119-21. The federal-tax-deduction percentage table and $5,000 cap were not re-checked against 2024 forms.

Montana.notes: 2025 Form 2: line 1 federal AGI (Form 1040 line 11b); line 2 = Form 1040 lines 12e + 13b (federal standard/itemized deduction plus Schedule 1-A deductions for qualified tips, qualified overtime, car-loan interest and the senior deduction - instructions state these 'are included in the calculation of Montana taxable income'); federal QBI deduction (13a) is NOT allowed. So Montana taxable income = federal taxable income (excl. QBI) +/- Schedule I adjustments; filer must use the same deduction type as federally. standard_deduction = 15,750 (2025 federal single SD under OBBBA). 2025 Montana ordinary income tax rates (single): TI < $21,100: 4.7%; TI >= $21,100: 5.9% x TI - $253 (exact bracket arithmetic gives $253.20). Value at $40k wages: TI 24,250 -> 991.70 + 5.9% x 3,150 = $1,177.55 (worksheet $1,177.75). Federal income tax deduction: 2024 instructions state Montana allowed an itemized deduction for federal income taxes paid only 'prior to the 2024 tax year' (eliminated by SB 399) - confirmed not available for 2024 or 2025. 2025 legislative changes for TY2025 are only 529-plan subtraction, military retirement subtraction sunset removal, NOL transition (HB 845, SB 53, SB 93, SB 544); HB 337 and HB 129 begin TY2026. No local income tax. Credits not included: MT EITC = 10% of federal EITC for 2025; Elderly Homeowner/Renter Credit (age 62+). $5,660 subtraction for age 65+ irrelevant. Discrepancy with Tax Foundation: TF standard deduction $15,000 (pre-OBBBA); correct embedded 2025 amount is $15,750. Brackets match TF.
Montana.changes_vs_2024: Threshold indexed: 2024 single 4.7% below $20,500, 5.9% above; 2025 4.7% below $21,100, 5.9% above. Rates unchanged (HB 337 rate/bracket changes start in TY2026; EITC rises to 20% in 2026). Embedded federal SD $14,600 (2024) -> $15,750 (2025), and OBBBA Schedule 1-A deductions (tips, overtime, car-loan interest, senior) flow through for 2025.

Nebraska.notes: All values from the official 2025 NE Tax Calculation Schedule (8-460-2025), 2025 Form 1040N and 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (8-307-2025). Computation: Form 1040N line 5 = federal AGI (Form 1040 line 11a); line 6 NE standard deduction $8,600 single (not tied to the federal amount; OBBBA's $15,750 does not flow through); line 14 NE taxable income = AGI - SD +/- Schedule I adjustments; tax from schedule; line 18 nonrefundable personal exemption credit $171 per exemption (residents), no income phase-out found in 2025 instructions. Value at $40k wages: TI 31,400; tax 804.30 + 5.01% x 7,280 = 1,169.03; minus $171 = $998.03. Special limit (line 35 Federal Tax Liability Worksheet): if net Schedule I adjustments < $5,000, NE tax after nonrefundable credits cannot exceed federal tax before credits (Form 1040 line 16 + Sch. 2 lines 2 and 8); not binding for a single wage earner at $20k+ under 2025 federal law (e.g., $20k wages: NE $186.83 vs federal $425). Because NE starts from federal AGI, the OBBBA below-the-line tips/overtime/senior/car-loan deductions (Schedule 1-A) do not reduce NE income; no NE Schedule I provision for them in the 2025 booklet. No local income taxes. Credits not included: NE EITC = 10% of federal EITC (refundable); child/dependent care credit; property-tax credits for school/community-college property taxes paid (property owners only). Matches Tax Foundation exactly (TF already had 2025 values).
Nebraska.changes_vs_2024: Top rate cut from 5.84% to 5.20% (LB 754 schedule). Single brackets indexed: 2024 = 2.46% to $3,900, 3.51% to $23,370, 5.01% to $37,670, 5.84% above; 2025 = 2.46% to $4,030, 3.51% to $24,120, 5.01% to $38,870, 5.20% above. Standard deduction $8,350 -> $8,600; personal exemption credit $166 -> $171. Material across $20k-$120k (top rate binds above ~$47.5k wages).

phaseouts.applies_to: total_tax_cap
phaseouts.formula: If Schedule I net adjustments < $5,000, NE tax after nonrefundable credits = min(NE tax after credits, federal tax before credits)

Nevada.notes: No individual income tax. The Modified Business Tax is levied on employers' payroll, not on employees. No local income taxes. starts_from is a placeholder.

New Hampshire.notes: No tax on wages in any year. The I&D Tax repeal is effective for taxable periods beginning after Dec 31, 2024; DRA states no 2025 I&D return is required. Verification note: revenue.nh.gov returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the DRA document (2023-003) was confirmed through its search-indexed text plus press coverage of the DRA's January 2025 reminder, not a direct fetch. Tax Foundation 2025 table also lists NH as 'none'. No local income taxes. starts_from is a placeholder.
New Hampshire.changes_vs_2024: Interest and Dividends Tax repealed for taxable periods beginning after Dec 31, 2024 (2023 HB 2, ch. 79, ss. 85-88). It never applied to wages, so no effect on the wage calculation. In 2024 the I&D rate was 3% on interest/dividend income above $2,400 (single).

New Jersey.notes: Source: 2025 NJ-1040 instructions (booklet labeled 2025; retrieved from the 'current' path, which will roll over to 2026 forms). Tax Rate Schedules p.63, Table A (Single), subtraction method: TI 0-20,000 x .014; 20,000-35,000 x .0175 - $70; 35,000-40,000 x .035 - $682.50; 40,000-75,000 x .05525 - $1,492.50; 75,000-500,000 x .0637 - $2,126.25; 500,000-1M x .0897 - $15,126.25; >1M x .1075 - $32,926.25. These are verified identical to the marginal brackets given. The tax table is required if TI < $100,000 (midpoint method; small differences). There is no standard deduction. The personal exemption is a $1,000 deduction ($1,000 more if 65+ or blind/disabled; $1,500 per dependent). The base is NJ gross income (state-defined income categories). NJ wages (W-2 box 16) can exceed federal box 1: contributions to retirement plans other than 401(k) (e.g. 403(b), 457, federal TSP) are included in NJ wages, while 401(k) contributions up to the federal limit are excluded. Federal tax is not deductible. Filing threshold: no return or tax if whole-year NJ gross income <= $10,000 (single). The instructions state this as a filing threshold, and the statutory basis is N.J.S.A. 54A:2-4 'Minimum taxable income' (statute text not retrieved). The cliff is irrelevant at $20k+. Examples (wages only): $20k: TI 19,000, $266. $40k: TI 39,000, $682.50. $80k: TI 79,000, $2,906. $120k: TI 119,000, $5,454. NOT INCLUDED but broadly available: the property tax deduction or credit for resident homeowners and tenants. The filer takes the better of a deduction of property taxes paid, up to $15,000 (for tenants, 18% of rent counts as property tax), or a $50 credit. Example: a renter paying $18,000/yr deducts $3,240, worth about $113 at $40k wages and $206 at $80k. NJ EITC not included. LOCAL: no resident local income tax. Newark's payroll tax is employer-paid, so 0. Tax Foundation 2025 matches.
New Jersey.changes_vs_2024: None. The 2024 NJ-1040 instructions have the same Table A schedule, the same $1,000 exemption and the same $10,000 single filing threshold.

phaseouts.applies_to: Low-income exemption / filing threshold (cliff, not a phase-out)
phaseouts.formula: If NJ gross income for the entire year <= $10,000 (single), no return is required and no tax is due. Above $10,000, tax applies to all taxable income with no phase-in.

New Mexico.notes: Starting point: federal AGI (PIT-1 line 9). Line 12 subtracts 'the allowable federal standard deduction from federal Form 1040 or 1040SR, line 12', which is $15,750 single for 2025 under OBBBA (NM has rolling conformity; the 2026 SB 151 decoupling concerns bonus depreciation/163(j)/NCTI, not the standard deduction). Federal Schedule 1-A deductions (tips/overtime/car loan/senior; Form 1040 line 13b) are not part of the NM computation. Brackets: statute NMSA 7-2-7(B) as amended by 2024 HB 252 for tax years beginning on or after 1/1/2025. Single: not over $5,500 is 1.5%; $82.50 + 3.2% over $5,500; $434.50 + 4.3% over $16,500; $1,165.50 + 4.7% over $33,500; $2,716.50 + 4.9% over $66,500; $9,748 + 5.9% over $210,000. The official 2025 tax rate table (PIT-TRT) matches these brackets to the dollar for every $100 row below $100,000. Discrepancy: for taxable income over $100,000 the TRT tells single filers to use '$4,356 plus 4.9% of excess over $100,000' and '$9,746 + 5.9% over $210,000'. Strict statute math gives $4,358 and $9,748, so the TRT is $2 lower above $100k. This is immaterial; it matters only at wages of about $115,750 or more. Low- and middle-income exemption (LMIE, line 14): single FAGI of $36,667 or less, (2,500 - 0.15 x (FAGI - 20,000)) per exemption. It materially affects $20k-$36k: $2,500 at $20k, $1,000 at $30k, $0 at $40k. It is set to 0 in 'personal_exemption' because the value at ~$40k is 0; see 'phaseouts'. Deduction of $4,000 per dependent beyond the first (HOH/MFJ only): n/a. Not included: the Low Income Comprehensive Tax Rebate (refundable; MGI up to $36,000; 2025 table, 1 exemption: $91 at MGI $19,501-$21,000, $17 at $34,001-$36,000) and the Working Families Tax Credit (state EITC). No local income taxes. Federal income tax is not deductible. Illustrative tax: $20k: taxable income 1,750 gives $26.25; $40k: TI 24,250 gives $767.75; $80k: TI 64,250 gives $2,610.75; $120k: TI 104,250 gives $4,566.25 by statute ($4,564.25 per the TRT formula). 2024 bracket values come from the prior statute text (Justia copy of NMSA 7-2-7), not an official 2024 TRD table. The 2024 LMIE formula was confirmed in the 2024 PIT-1 instructions (NBER mirror). Tax Foundation discrepancies: TF brackets match 2025 law. TF standard deduction is $15,000; official 2025 is $15,750. TF omits the LMIE.

phaseouts.applies_to: low_and_middle_income_exemption (deduction, PIT-1 line 14)
phaseouts.formula: If FAGI (PIT-1 line 9) <= 36667 (single): exemption = max(0, 2500 - 0.15 * max(0, FAGI - 20000)) * number_of_federal_exemptions (1 for single, no dependents); else 0.

New Mexico.changes_vs_2024: There are new 2025 brackets (2024 HB 252, Laws 2024 ch. 67). 2024 single was 1.7% up to $5,500, 3.2% on $5,500-$11,000, 4.7% on $11,000-$16,000, 4.9% on $16,000-$210,000, and 5.9% above $210,000 (prior NMSA 7-2-7). 2025 single is 1.5% / 3.2% from $5,500 / 4.3% from $16,500 / 4.7% from $33,500 / 4.9% from $66,500 / 5.9% from $210,000. The federal standard deduction rose from $14,600 to $15,750. The LMIE formula is unchanged. At $40k wages, tax falls from $965.10 (2024) to $767.75 (2025), a large relative cut in the $20k-$80k range.

New York.notes: Source: 2025 IT-201-I, NYS tax rate schedule p.33, single: $0-8,500 4%; 8,500-11,700 $340+4.5%; 11,700-13,900 $484+5.25%; 13,900-80,650 $600+5.5%; 80,650-215,400 $4,271+6%; 215,400-1,077,550 $12,356+6.85%; 1,077,550-5M $71,413+9.65%; 5M-25M $449,929+10.3%; >25M $2,509,929+10.9%. The base amounts equal the cumulative marginal tax rounded to whole dollars, so the plain brackets reproduce the schedule. If NY AGI <= $107,650 and TI < $65,000, the filer must use the NYS tax table instead (midpoint method; differs from the schedule by about $1-3). Standard deduction $8,000 for a single filer who cannot be claimed as a dependent ($3,100 if claimable). There is no exemption for the filer; the $1,000 exemption applies per dependent only. Income starts from federal AGI (IT-201 line 19), adjusted by NY additions and subtractions to give NY AGI (line 33). Federal tax is not deductible. RECAPTURE: see the 'recapture' key. It matters inside $20k-$120k only above $107,650 NY AGI, adding $140 at $120k wages. Examples (schedule, wages only): $20k: TI 12,000, tax $499.75, minus $45 household credit = $454.75. $40k: TI 32,000, $1,595. $80k: TI 72,000, $3,795. $120k: TI 112,000, $6,292 including recapture. Filing is required if a federal return is required or federal AGI plus NY additions exceeds $4,000. LOCAL: typical_local_income_tax_rate 0.0168 is the Tax Foundation 2025 footnote (a) statewide average effective local income tax as a percentage of AGI (2022 IRS/Census data). Actual local income tax applies only to NYC and Yonkers residents and is 0 elsewhere in the state. NYC: see nyc_resident_brackets (2025 rates 3.078% / 3.762% / 3.819% / 3.876%; about $1,126 at $40k wages before school tax credits). Yonkers resident surcharge = 16.75% of net NYS tax (IT-201-I Yonkers worksheet). NYS and NYC earned income credits are not included. Tax Foundation 2025 matches the official 2025 schedule and standard deduction exactly.
New York.changes_vs_2024: None material. The 2024 IT-201-I has the same single schedule, $8,000 standard deduction, $107,650 recapture threshold, household credit table 1 and NYC rate schedule (NY brackets are not indexed). The FY2026 budget cuts the five lowest rates by 0.1 point for TY2026 and another 0.1 point for TY2027 (secondary source: governor's budget page). That does not affect 2025, and the 2025 IT-201-I schedule is unchanged.

recapture.formula: For NY AGI > 107,650 and TI <= 215,400 (Tax computation worksheet 7): tax = S + (0.06*TI - S) * min(1, round((NYAGI - 107650)/50000, 4)), where S = rate-schedule tax on TI. If NY AGI >= 157,650 the tax is 6% of all TI. Higher worksheets (8-11) apply only when TI > 215,400.

phaseouts.applies_to: NYS household credit (nonrefundable; single filers who cannot be claimed as a dependent)
phaseouts.formula: Credit by federal AGI, table 1 (upper bounds inclusive)

nyc_resident_brackets.base: NYC taxable income (IT-201 line 47); for a full-year resident taking the standard deduction this equals NY taxable income
nyc_resident_brackets.credits: NYC school tax credit, fixed amount: $63 (single, income <= $250,000; refundable). NYC school tax credit, rate-reduction amount (single): 0.171% of NYC TI up to $12,000; $21 + 0.228% of the excess over $12,000 (income <= $500,000). The net NYC rates after the rate-reduction amount are 2.907% / 3.534% / 3.591% / 3.648%. NYC household credit (single): $15 if federal AGI <= $10,000; $10 if <= $12,500; none above.
nyc_resident_brackets.source: IT-201-I (2025), New York City tax rate schedule p.40; school tax credit pp.20-21; NYC household credit table 4 p.14

North Carolina.notes: Source: 2025 Form D-401 instructions: 'For tax year 2025, the individual income tax rate is 4.25%... multiply your North Carolina taxable income by 4.25%'. The NC standard deduction chart (D-400 Schedule A/D-401) gives single $12,750, flat with no phase-out. It is $0 only if the filer is ineligible for a federal standard deduction. No personal exemption. Starting point is federal AGI. No federal tax deduction, no low-income credit, no state EITC. Same values at $20k/$40k/$80k/$120k. Example: $40k wages gives (40,000 - 12,750) x 4.25% = $1,158.13. Matches Tax Foundation exactly. Conformity: the 2025 D-401 said the starting point was federal AGI under the IRC as of Jan 1, 2023 and that NC does not follow the federal standard deduction or the Schedule 1-A deductions. Session Law 2026-31 (enacted July 2026) later moved the IRC reference to July 5, 2025, effective for 2025. NCDOR's FAQ (updated Oct 9, 2026) confirms: (Q14) the OBBBA tips, overtime, car-loan and senior deductions do NOT reduce NC taxable income for 2025, and (Q15) the NC standard deduction did NOT increase for 2025. No 2026 law changed the 2025 rate. Separately, the rate is scheduled to drop to 3.99% for 2026 under existing law (secondary source; not needed for 2025). No local income taxes.
North Carolina.changes_vs_2024: Rate fell from 4.5% (2024 D-401) to 4.25% (2025). The single standard deduction stays at $12,750 and there is no personal exemption in either year. Effect: 0.25 points on taxable income, e.g. about $68 less at $40k wages ($27,250 taxable).

North Dakota.notes: 2025 ND-1 booklet: ND starts from federal taxable income (Form 1040 line 15; ND-1 line 1b) and 'perpetually conforms' to the computation of federal taxable income; the booklet states the OBBBA increased standard deduction, $6,000 senior deduction, $40,000 SALT cap and 'Tip income and overtime pay exclusions' are included in ND's starting point by default (ND did NOT decouple). standard_deduction = 15,750 = 2025 federal single SD (IRS IR release) embedded in federal taxable income; ND has no separate SD or exemption. 2025 Tax Rate Schedule (single): 0-48,475 at 0%; 48,475-244,825: 1.95% of excess; over 244,825: $3,828.83 + 2.50% (tax tables for TI < $100k). Value at $40k wages: FTI 24,250 -> $0. At $120k wages: FTI 104,250 -> 1.95% x 55,775 = $1,087.61. No local income tax. Discrepancies with Tax Foundation: (1) TF footnote (j) says bracket widths are 2024 values, but TF's $48,475/$244,825 are in fact the official 2025 thresholds (2024 were $47,150/$238,200) - so TF numbers are right, footnote is wrong for ND; (2) TF standard deduction $15,000 is the pre-OBBBA federal amount; correct embedded 2025 amount is $15,750. Federal tips deduction (max $25,000) and overtime deduction (max $12,500 single), phased out above $150,000 MAGI single, reduce ND income if claimed federally.
North Dakota.changes_vs_2024: Brackets indexed: 2024 single 0% to $47,150, 1.95% to $238,200, 2.50% above; 2025 0% to $48,475, 1.95% to $244,825. Embedded federal standard deduction rose from $14,600 (2024) to $15,750 (2025, OBBBA). Also the federal tips/overtime/senior/car-loan deductions flow through for 2025. Combined effect: zero ND tax for single wage earners up to $64,225 wages (vs $61,750 in 2024).

Ohio.notes: Rates/brackets: 2025 IT 1040 booklet p.18 ('2025 Ohio Income Tax Brackets') and R.C. 5747.02(A)(3)(b) (effective 9/30/2025, HB 96). CRITICAL: Ohio's schedule has base amounts that a plain marginal-rate calculator will miss. Use alt_brackets/phaseouts[0]: tax = 0 if TI <= 26,050; 342.00 + 2.75%*(TI-26,050) up to 100,000; 2,394.32 + 3.125%*(TI-100,000) above. The $342 = 1.31287% x $26,050 (statutory). Ignoring the base understates tax by $342 for everyone above $26,050 TI (about half the liability at $40k). No standard deduction. Personal exemption is a deduction by MAGI tier: $2,400 (MAGI <= $40,000), $2,150 ($40,001-$80,000), $1,900 ($80,001-$749,999), $0 ($750,000+). These are cliffs, so $40,000 exactly gets $2,400 and $40,001 gets $2,150. Exemption credit: $20 per exemption if MAGI less exemptions < $30,000 (R.C. 5747.022), which matters only at the low end ($20k wages). Joint filing credit not applicable to singles. Ohio EITC (30% of federal EIC, nonrefundable) excluded. Ohio starts from federal AGI (IT 1040 line 1), so the federal OBBBA tips/overtime deductions (below-AGI, Schedule 1-A) do not flow into Ohio. Check values (wages = AGI): $20k: TI 17,600, tax 0. $40k: TI 37,600, tax $659.63. $80k: exemption 2,150, TI 77,850, tax $1,766.50. $120k: exemption 1,900, TI 118,100, tax $2,959.95. LOCAL: typical_local_income_tax_rate = Tax Foundation footnote (a) statewide average effective local income tax of 1.49% of AGI (2022 IRS/Census data), covering municipal plus school district income taxes. Municipal income taxes apply to wages at the work location, with resident credits that vary by city. Statutory resident rates: Columbus 2.5% (city IR-25 instructions, seen only via search result because columbus.gov returned 403), Cleveland 2.5% (CCA tax rate table, ccaohio.gov/tax-rates), Cincinnati 1.8% since 10/2/2020 (cincinnati-oh.gov). Many other cities levy 1.0%-2.5%, often 2.0%-2.5%. I found no official statewide municipal rate file for 2025 (ODT LG-11 tables stop at CY2018). School district income tax: per the 2025 booklet SD list, 210 of 611 school districts levy an SD income tax (146 traditional base = Ohio taxable income, 64 earned-income base). Rates run 0.25%-2.0%, mean 1.10%, median 1.00%. DISCREPANCIES WITH TAX FOUNDATION: (1) TF shows the 3.5% top rate (pre-HB 96); 2025 law is 3.125%. (2) TF lists only marginal rates and omits the $342 / $2,394.32 base amounts, so a TF-based calculation understates Ohio tax by about $342. (3) TF footnote (dd) omits the $0 exemption tier at MAGI >= $750,000 (irrelevant for $20k-$120k).

phaseouts.applies_to: tax_schedule_base_amount
phaseouts.formula: TI = Ohio AGI - exemptions (nonbusiness income). tax = 0 if TI <= 26050; tax = 342.00 + 0.0275*(TI - 26050) if 26050 < TI <= 100000; tax = 2394.32 + 0.03125*(TI - 100000) if TI > 100000. The base amounts are NOT the cumulative tax of the lower brackets: there is a $342 notch at TI = $26,050 and an $18.69 notch at TI = $100,000 (2394.32 vs 342 + 0.0275*73950 = 2375.63).

phaseouts.applies_to: personal_exemption
phaseouts.formula: Exemption per person is a step function of Ohio MAGI (= Ohio AGI + business income deduction; equals Ohio AGI for a wage earner).

phaseouts.applies_to: exemption_credit
phaseouts.formula: Nonrefundable credit of $20 per exemption claimed if (Ohio MAGI - exemption amount) < $30,000 (R.C. 5747.022). Single, no dependents: $20 if MAGI less exemption < 30000, else 0.

Ohio.changes_vs_2024: Material. HB 96 (136th GA, signed 6/30/2025) cut the top rate from 3.5% to 3.125% for TY2025 and reduced the base amount for the 2.75% bracket from $360.69 to $342.00. 2024 schedule: 0 to $26,050 = 0; $26,050-$100,000 = $360.69 + 2.75% of excess; over $100,000 = $2,394.32 + 3.5% of excess. So every single filer with TI over $26,050 pays $18.69 less in 2025, and filers over $100,000 also get the lower 3.125% marginal rate. Exemption tiers ($2,400/$2,150/$1,900) and the $20 exemption credit are unchanged from 2024. Statute also sets TY2026+ at a flat $332.00 + 2.75% of TI over $26,050 (not used here).

Oklahoma.notes: The source URL is OTC's '/current/' path. The file downloaded on 2026-10-17 is titled '2025 Oklahoma Resident Individual Income Tax Forms and Instructions' (contains the 2025 Income Tax Tables), but this path will roll over to the 2026 packet. The packet does not print a rate schedule. It gives a tax table for taxable income under $100,000 and, for single filers at $100,000 or more, '$4,562 plus 0.0475 over $100,000'. The brackets above (the statutory 0.25%-4.75% schedule) are derived from that table: a script check reproduced all 1,999 $50 rows of the official 2025 single/MFS column ($0-$100,000) exactly at band midpoints, and the schedule gives $4,561.50, which rounds to $4,562, at $100,000. Computation: federal AGI (Form 511 line 1) plus or minus Oklahoma adjustments, minus the standard deduction, minus exemptions. The standard deduction is a fixed $6,350 for single/MFS, not tied to the federal amount; a filer who takes the federal standard deduction must take Oklahoma's. The exemption is a $1,000 deduction per exemption. The extra 'special' exemption is only for age 65+ with federal AGI <= $15,000 (single). Federal income tax is not deductible. Tips and overtime: the 2025 packet has no Oklahoma subtraction for them, and the federal deductions are below AGI, so they do not affect Oklahoma. Credits not included in the numbers: the Sales Tax Relief Credit (Form 538-S, refundable, $40 per exemption), whose gross household income limit is $20,000 for a single filer under 65 with no dependents, so a $20k wage earner is right at the limit; and the Oklahoma EIC (5% of federal EIC under 2020 rules). Oklahoma has no local income taxes. Illustrative 2025 tax (schedule): $20k wages = TI $12,650, about $412; $40k = TI $32,650, about $1,362 (table $1,364); $80k = about $3,262; $120k = TI $112,650, $4,562 + 4.75% x $12,650 = about $5,163. No discrepancies with Tax Foundation (TF: 0.25%-4.75%, $6,350, $1,000).
Oklahoma.changes_vs_2024: None material. The 2024 Form 511 packet has the same $6,350 single standard deduction, $1,000 exemption, identical tax-table values (e.g. $1,713 at $40,000-$40,050) and the same '$4,562 plus 0.0475 over $100,000' rule. HB 2764 (2025) cuts the top rate to 4.5% and consolidates brackets starting tax year 2026 (per the legislature's fiscal impact statement and press coverage), so it does not affect 2025.

Oregon.notes: Brackets, standard deduction, exemption credit and federal-tax-subtraction cap come from the 'Miscellaneous Oregon income tax information for tax years 2022-2025' table in Publication OR-17 (2025, rev. 01-29-26). 2025 single: 4.75% up to $4,400; 6.75% on $4,401-$11,100; 8.75% on $11,101-$125,000; 9.9% over $125,000. Cross-check: 2025 OR-40 instructions Chart S gives '$4,065 plus 8.75% of excess over $50,000' for $50k-$125k and '$10,627 plus 9.9% of excess over $125,000', consistent with those brackets. Taxable income below $50,000 uses $100-row tax tables. Standard deduction: $2,835 single (state-defined, not federal; no phase-out). Exemption credit: $256, nonrefundable; zero if federal AGI exceeds $100,000 single. So the credit is lost for wages above $100k within the $20k-$120k range. Starting point: federal AGI. Oregon has a rolling tie to the federal taxable income definition, so 2025 allows the federal tips/overtime/car-loan-interest deductions (not modeled). The 2026 SB 1507 disconnect from car-loan interest and other items is TY2026+ (secondary sources). Federal tax subtraction: up to $8,500 for 2025, AGI-limited per OR-40 instructions Table 4 (see 'federal_tax_deduction'). Illustrative (federal tax computed with 2025 federal brackets and $15,750 standard deduction; Oregon tax computed by formula, so the tables may differ by a few dollars): $20k: fed tax $425, OR TI $16,740, tax $898.75; $40k: fed tax $2,671.50, OR TI $34,493.50, tax $2,708.18 - $256 = $2,452.18; $80k: fed tax $9,049, subtraction capped at $8,500, OR TI $68,665, tax $5,442.19 after credit; $120k: subtraction $8,500, OR TI $108,665, no exemption credit (AGI > $100k), tax $9,198.19. Kicker: 2025 returns claim a refundable surplus credit of 9.863% of the filer's 2024 Oregon liability (line 32). It is a one-time refund of prior-year tax, not a 2025 rate parameter, and is not included, but it materially lowers 2025 net payments for filers who had 2024 liability. Local: the Metro Supportive Housing Services tax is 1% of Metro taxable income above $125,000 single ($200,000 joint); 2025 thresholds are not indexed (indexing starts TY2026). The Multnomah County Preschool for All tax is 1.5% above $125,000 single plus an additional 1.5% above $250,000. Both bite only when Oregon taxable income exceeds $125k, which does not happen at wages of $120k or less (OR TI is about $108.7k at $120k wages). Hence typical_local_income_tax_rate = 0. Statewide transit tax (ORS 320.550): 0.1% of wages, employee-paid and withheld by the employer. It is a payroll-type tax and is not included in brackets; add 0.001 x wages if desired. Not included: Oregon EITC and the working family household and dependent care credit. Tax Foundation discrepancies: TF shows 6.75% from $4,400 and 8.75% from $11,050. Official 2025 is $4,400 and $11,100; TF footnote (bb) labels these as 2025-adjusted, but the second threshold is $50 low. TF std deduction $2,800 vs official 2025 $2,835 (official 2024 was $2,745). TF exemption credit $250 vs official 2025 $256 (2024 was $249). TF does not give the federal-tax-subtraction cap.

federal_tax_deduction.amount_definition: Federal income tax liability after nonrefundable credits (Form 1040 line 22), minus excess APTC repayment (Sch. 2 line 1a), plus income-tax-only items from Sch. 2 lines 8/16/17, minus refundable AOTC, refundable adoption credit and premium tax credit (not EITC); then limited to the AGI-based maximum. Uses the actual 2025 federal return (OBBBA $15,750 federal standard deduction).
federal_tax_deduction.phaseout_note: agi_max is exclusive ('at least X but less than Y'). Single and HOH/MFJ use different tables; the single table is shown.

phaseouts.applies_to: personal_exemption_credit
phaseouts.formula: credit = 256 per regular exemption if federal AGI <= 100000 (single); 0 if federal AGI > 100000 (cliff, not a gradual phase-out). Nonrefundable.

Oregon.changes_vs_2024: Brackets were indexed: 2024 single 4.75% up to $4,300, 6.75% on $4,301-$10,750, 8.75% on $10,751-$125,000, 9.9% above that. 2025 is $4,400 / $11,100 / $125,000. Standard deduction rose from $2,745 to $2,835. The exemption credit rose from $249 to $256. The federal tax subtraction cap rose from $8,250 to $8,500, with the AGI phase-out unchanged. Federal liability in 2025 is lower (OBBBA standard deduction), which slightly shrinks the subtraction. Net effect is a small decrease in tax at $20k-$120k. Separately, 2025 returns carry a one-time kicker credit (9.863% of 2024 liability); see notes.

Pennsylvania.notes: Source: 2025 PA-40 IN booklet: 'The state income tax rate for 2025 is 3.07 percent (0.0307).' PA law allows no standard deduction, no personal exemption and no itemized deductions (PA-40 IN 'Deductions'). Tax applies to the sum of state-defined income classes: compensation net of allowable unreimbursed employee business expenses, interest, dividends, net business profits, gains, rents/royalties, estate/trust income and gambling winnings. A loss in one class cannot offset income in another. Allowed deductions are limited to Schedule O items (e.g. 529/ABLE contributions, and new for 2025 student loan interest up to $2,500). Federal tax is not deductible. A return is required if PA gross taxable income > $33. TAX FORGIVENESS: see phaseouts. Forgiveness is 100% at eligibility income <= $6,500 and falls 10 points per $250 to 10% at <= $8,750, so it is irrelevant at $20k+ wages. The Working Pennsylvanians Tax Credit (10% of federal EITC, refundable, applies to TY2025 per pa.gov/secondary reports) is not included. A childless single filer at >= $20k wages is above the 2025 federal EITC phase-out (about $19.1k; figure not re-verified here). Example: $40k wages = $1,228. LOCAL: typical_local_income_tax_rate 0.0107 is the Tax Foundation footnote (a) statewide average effective local income tax as a percentage of AGI (2022 data). Statutory picture: nearly all municipalities and school districts levy a resident Earned Income Tax (Act 32 collection). The Act 511 base cap is 1% shared between municipality and school district, so a 1% combined rate is common, though many jurisdictions exceed it under other statutes (secondary sources; no statewide rate register was pulled). Philadelphia resident Wage Tax (phila.gov): 3.75% from July 1, 2024 and 3.74% from July 1, 2025 (non-resident 3.44% / 3.43%), so about 3.745% for calendar 2025. The resident rate falls to 3.735% from July 1, 2026. Residents eligible for PA tax forgiveness pay 1.5%. Pittsburgh residents pay 3% EIT (1% city + 2% school district) per pittsburghpa.gov. Local Services Tax: up to $52/yr (Pittsburgh: $52), levied by the municipality of the work site, not the residence. Municipalities levying more than $10 must exempt people earning under $12,000 there (secondary: municipal ordinances under the Local Tax Enabling Act). The LST is a per-capita levy, not an income-rate tax, so it is excluded from the rate. The local EIT base (earned income) differs slightly from the PA compensation base. Tax Foundation 2025 matches.
Pennsylvania.changes_vs_2024: State: none (3.07% in both the 2024 and 2025 PA-40 booklets). New 2025 deduction of up to $2,500 of student loan interest (Schedule O). New refundable Working Pennsylvanians Tax Credit (10% of federal EITC; EITC-type, not included). Local: the Philadelphia resident wage tax fell from 3.75% to 3.74% for pay dated after June 30, 2025.

phaseouts.applies_to: Tax Forgiveness (Schedule SP), unmarried claimant with no dependents
phaseouts.formula: Percentage of PA tax forgiven by eligibility income (Eligibility Income Table 1)

Rhode Island.notes: 2025 uniform schedule for all filing statuses (RI Division of Taxation '2025 Tax Rate Schedule and Worksheets'; also RI ADV 2024-26 dated Oct 31, 2024): 0-79,900 at 3.75%; 79,900-181,650 is $2,996.25 + 4.75% over 79,900; > 181,650 is $7,829.38 + 5.99%. Tax tables apply at lower incomes; the schedule is used above the table range, with only rounding differences. Standard deduction (RI-1040 line 4): $10,900 single. It is state-defined and indexed, not tied to federal. RI does not allow federal itemized deductions. Exemption (line 6): $5,100 per exemption, a deduction. Phase-out of both the standard deduction and the exemption, on modified federal AGI (RI-1040 line 3): if MAGI <= $254,250, full amount. Otherwise n = ceil((MAGI - 254,250)/7,250) and the amount is multiplied by 0.8, 0.6, 0.4 or 0.2 for n = 1-4. If the excess is > $29,000 (MAGI > $283,250), the amount is zero. This does not bind at <= $120k. Starting point: federal AGI (RI-1040 line 1) +/- RI Schedule M modifications. For 2025 RI decoupled from certain OBBBA business provisions via new Schedule HR1 (163(j), 174A, 179(b), 181). These are irrelevant to wage earners. Example at $40k wages: taxable = 40,000 - 10,900 - 5,100 = 24,000; tax = $900. Not included: RI earned income credit (refundable; percentage of the federal EITC) and the RI-1040H property tax relief credit (income-limited). No local income taxes. Source note: the official RI-1040 instructions PDF is byte-identical (SHA-256) to the NBER mirror copy. No discrepancies with Tax Foundation.
Rhode Island.changes_vs_2024: Inflation indexing. 2024: brackets 3.75% to $77,450; 4.75% $77,450-$176,050; 5.99% above. Standard deduction $10,550 single; exemption $4,950; phase-out range $246,450-$274,650 in $7,050 steps. 2025: $79,900 / $181,650; $10,900; $5,100; $254,250-$283,250 in $7,250 steps. This lowers tax slightly across $20k-$120k.

South Carolina.notes: Rates and brackets come from the 2025 SC1040TT tax tables (revised 6/17/25). Table spot checks: tax is $405 at $17,000-$17,100 [3% x (17,050 - 3,560)] and $561 at $20,000-$20,100 [428.10 + 6% x (20,050 - 17,830)]. For taxable income of $100,000 or more, the rate schedule is 6% x TI - $642, consistent with the 3,560/17,830 breaks. Below $100,000 tax comes from tables in $50/$100 bands priced at the band midpoint. SCDOR's individual income page and IL 25-11 (Proviso 117.208 suspends the 12-6-510(B) phase-down: 'The top marginal income tax rate is 6% for the 2025 tax year') confirm the rate. Discrepancy with Tax Foundation: TF shows a 6.2% top rate (footnote qq cites 2025 withholding tables). Correct 2025 rate is 6.0%. TF thresholds ($3,560/$17,830) match. Starting point: SC1040 line 1 is federal taxable income, so the federal standard deduction is built in. There is no SC personal exemption (the federal exemption is $0). The SC dependent exemption is $4,930 for 2025 (TF showed the 2024 $4,790), irrelevant for no dependents. OBBBA conformity: SC conforms to the IRC as amended through Dec 31, 2024 (S.507, Act 63 of 2025). SC Information Letter #26-4 (Revised, Jan 30, 2026) lists items SC taxpayers must add back for 2025. These include the $750 single increase in the federal standard deduction (so SC effectively allows $15,000 = $15,750 - $750), the $6,000 senior deduction, and the tips (up to $25,000), overtime (up to $12,500) and car-loan interest deductions. H.3368, which would have conformed SC to the IRC through Dec 31, 2025 for 2025, failed second reading in the Senate 16-27 on March 31, 2026. The companion bills (H.5167, H.5178) are still in committee. SCDOR extended the 2025 filing deadline to Oct 15, 2026 while the bill was pending. As of this check (Oct 2026), the SCDOR individual-income page still states Dec 31, 2024 conformity for 2025, and IL 26-4 (Rev.) is the latest conformity guidance. So the calculator should use SC taxable income = federal AGI - $15,000 (single, standard deduction), with no tips/overtime deduction. The standard deduction is not phased. Same parameters at $20k/$40k/$80k/$120k. Examples: $20k wages gives TI $5,000 and table tax about $44. $40k wages gives TI $25,000 and table tax about $861. Act 110 of 2026 (H.4216: 1.99%/5.21% brackets, start from federal AGI, new SC Income Adjusted Deduction) applies only to tax years after 2025 (IL 26-20). Credits: SC EITC (nonrefundable, SC1040TC) not modeled. The two-wage-earner credit is for married couples only. No local income taxes. verified = true: rates, brackets and the standard deduction treatment come from official SCDOR documents. Residual caveat: a later retroactive conformity act would change the $15,000 and tips/overtime treatment, but none was found as of Oct 17, 2026.
South Carolina.changes_vs_2024: Top rate cut from 6.2% (2024) to 6.0% (2025) by FY2025-26 budget Proviso 117.208 (H.4025, Act 69 of 2025). Indexed thresholds rose from 3% over $3,460 and 6.2% over $17,330 (2024 SC1040TT) to 3% over $3,560 and 6% over $17,830 (2025 SC1040TT). The embedded federal standard deduction rose from $14,600 (2024) to $15,000 (2025, pre-OBBBA amount, since SC did not adopt the OBBBA $15,750). Net: at $40k wages (single, standard deduction), 2025 SC table tax is $861 (TI $25,000) vs $919 for 2024 (TI $25,400; 2024 table).

The Hall income tax (interest/dividends only, never wages) was repealed for tax years beginning on or after Jan 1, 2021. tn.gov returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; repeal confirmed through TN DOR help-center article HIT-3 and DOR pages as indexed in search. Utah.notes: All values come from the 2025 TC-40 Forms and Instructions. Rate: What's New says 'The 2025 Utah Legislature passed HB 106, lowering the income tax rate from 4.55 percent to 4.5 percent.' Line 10 multiplies Utah taxable income by 4.5%. Utah has no standard deduction or personal exemption for the filer. Instead, the nonrefundable taxpayer tax credit applies (lines 11-20): 6% of (Utah personal exemptions for dependents at $2,111 each + the federal standard or itemized deduction from the federal return, less state income tax included in federal itemized deductions). The credit is reduced by 1.3% of Utah taxable income above the base phase-out amount of $18,213 single. The credit uses the actual 2025 federal standard deduction from the federal return, i.e. the OBBBA $15,750. The TC-40 line-21 worksheet explicitly uses 'Single: Enter $15,750'. Single, no dependents: initial credit = $945, fully phased out at $90,905 of income. At ~$40k wages: credit $661.77, tax $1,138.23 (effective 2.85%). At $20k: gross tax $900 less credit $921.77 gives $0. At $80k: $3,458.23. At $120k: $5,400. The 'standard_deduction 0' and brackets above must be combined with the taxpayer-credit phaseout to get correct liabilities. Qualified exempt taxpayer: tax is $0 if FAGI is at or below the federal standard deduction. No new 2025 credits apply to all single filers. HB 106 expanded child tax credit eligibility (dependents only) and created employer childcare credits. The Utah EITC (nonrefundable, for low-income filers with qualifying children) is not relevant/not included. No local income taxes. Federal income tax is not deductible. Forward-looking (secondary sources only, not verified officially): 2026 SB 60 reportedly cuts the rate to 4.45% for TY2026; TY2025 is unaffected. URL caveat: tax.utah.gov/forms/current/ will roll to the 2026 forms; the copy used is titled '2025 TC-40 Forms and Instructions'. Tax Foundation discrepancies: TF shows 4.55% (pre-HB 106); official 2025 is 4.5%. TF shows a '$900 credit' (6% x $15,000); official 2025 is $945 (6% x $15,750). TF footnote (gg) phase-out base is $17,652 (2024); 2025 is $18,213. TF dependent exemption is $2,046 (2024); 2025 is $2,111.

phaseouts.applies_to: taxpayer_tax_credit (nonrefundable; functions as the standard deduction/personal exemption)
phaseouts.formula: credit = max(0, 0.06 * (federal_standard_or_itemized_deduction - state_income_tax_itemized + 2111 * n_dependents) - 0.013 * max(0, utah_taxable_income - base_phaseout)); utah_tax = max(0, 0.045 * utah_taxable_income - credit). Utah taxable income = FAGI + additions - subtractions (TC-40 line 9); equals FAGI for a plain wage earner.

phaseouts.applies_to: qualified_exempt_taxpayer
phaseouts.formula: If FAGI <= federal standard deduction ($15,750 single, excluding extra age/blind amounts) + federal enhanced senior deduction, Utah income tax = 0.

Utah.changes_vs_2024: The rate fell from 4.55% to 4.5% (2025 HB 106). The taxpayer-credit base phase-out amount rose from $17,652 to $18,213. The federal standard deduction feeding the credit rose from $14,600 to $15,750, so the initial credit went from $876 to $945. The dependent exemption rose from $2,046 to $2,111 (n/a here). At $40k wages, tax falls from $1,234.52 (2024) to $1,138.23 (2025).

Vermont.notes: 2025 single Schedule X (Vermont Dept. of Taxes 2025 Tax Rate Schedules, also printed in the 2025 IN-111 instructions): 0-49,400 at 3.35%; 49,400-119,700 is $1,655 + 6.60% over 49,400; 119,700-249,700 is $6,295 + 7.60% over 119,700; > 249,700 is $16,175 + 8.75% over 249,700. Taxable income under $75,000 must use the tax tables (midpoint method; tiny rounding differences). Standard deduction (IN-111 line 4): $7,650 single, plus $1,250 per federal age/blind box. It is state-defined and indexed, not tied to the federal amount, so OBBBA's $15,750 is irrelevant. Personal exemption (line 5e): $5,300 per exemption, a deduction. Starting point: federal AGI (IN-111 line 1) +/- Schedule IN-112 modifications. Minimum tax: if federal AGI > $150,000, tax = max(schedule tax, 3% x (federal AGI - U.S. obligation interest)). This does not bind at <= $120k. Example at $40k wages: taxable = 40,000 - 7,650 - 5,300 = 27,050; tax = 3.35% = $906. Not included: Vermont EITC (refundable), Renter Credit (RCC-146, income-limited), Social Security exclusion. No local income taxes on wages. Discrepancy with TF: TF's VT brackets ($47,900/$116,000/$242,000), standard deduction ($7,400) and exemption ($5,100) are 2024 values (TF footnotes j and n). The correct 2025 values are $49,400/$119,700/$249,700, $7,650 and $5,300.
Vermont.changes_vs_2024: Inflation indexing. 2024 single: 3.35% to $47,900; 6.6% $47,900-$116,000; 7.6% $116,000-$242,000; 8.75% above $242,000. Standard deduction $7,400; exemption $5,100. 2025: brackets at $49,400 / $119,700 / $249,700; standard deduction $7,650; exemption $5,300. Combined standard deduction plus exemption rises $450, and the 6.6% bracket starts $1,500 higher. This lowers tax slightly across $20k-$120k.

Virginia.notes: Source: 2025 Form 760 resident instructions (they reflect 2026 session changes). Rate schedule: 2% up to $3,000; $60 + 3% over $3,000; $120 + 5% over $5,000; $720 + 5.75% over $17,000. The instructions' example: $90,000 taxable gives $4,918. The 2025 single standard deduction is $8,750 ('Legislation enacted during the 2025 General Assembly session increased the standard deduction for Taxable Years 2025 and 2026 from $8,500 to $8,750 for single filers'), with no phase-out. It must be taken if the federal standard deduction was claimed. The personal exemption is $930 per exemption, a deduction (an extra $800 for age 65+/blind). Starting point: federal AGI, adjusted on Schedule ADJ to Virginia AGI. Conformity: the 2026 amendments to the 2025 Appropriation Act set a fixed conformity date of Dec 31, 2025, so VA conforms to most OBBBA provisions as they affect federal AGI and itemized deductions. The federal tips, overtime, car-loan and senior deductions are taken below AGI and have no Virginia counterpart (no such subtraction appears in the 2025 instructions), so they do not reduce VA tax. Not deductible: federal income tax. Same values at $20k/$40k/$80k/$120k. Example: $40k wages gives TI 40,000 - 8,750 - 930 = 30,320 and tax = 720 + 5.75% x 13,320 = $1,485.90. Discrepancy with Tax Foundation: TF lists the 2024 $8,500 standard deduction; correct 2025 value is $8,750. Rates and exemption match TF. Low-income items (not modeled): the filing threshold is VAGI $11,950 single (below it tax is $0). The nonrefundable Credit for Low-Income Individuals ($300 per exemption) needs family VAGI at or below the 2025 poverty guideline, $15,650 for one person, so it does not apply at $20k+ wages. The VA EITC (refundable portion raised to 20% of the federal EITC for 2025-2026) is EITC-type and excluded. No local income taxes on wages in Virginia.
Virginia.changes_vs_2024: Single standard deduction rose from $8,500 (2024) to $8,750 (2025; 2025 General Assembly legislation, for TY2025-2026, scheduled to revert to $3,000 after 2026). Rates, brackets and the $930 exemption are unchanged. Effect: $250 x 5.75% = about $14 less tax for any single filer above about $26k wages.

Washington.notes: No tax on wages for 2025. The capital gains excise tax is outside the scope of a wage calculation. WA Cares long-term-care payroll premium (0.58% of employee wages) is a payroll tax, not an income tax, and is excluded. DOR's income-tax page (fetched Oct 2026) also states that a new 9.9% income tax on annual AGI above $1 million begins Jan 1, 2028; it does not affect 2025 and is far above the $20k-$120k range. starts_from is a placeholder.
Washington.changes_vs_2024: No change for wages. Capital gains tax (not wages) gained a second tier for 2025: 7% on taxable long-term capital gains up to $1 million plus an additional 2.9% (9.9% total) above $1 million (ESSB 5813, ch. 421, Laws of 2025); 2025 capital gains standard deduction $278,000 (2024: $270,000).

West Virginia.notes: Official 2025 Rate Schedule I (single/HoH/MFJ): under $10,000, 2.22%; $10,000-$25,000, $222 + 2.96% of the excess over $10,000; $25,000-$40,000, $666 + 3.33%; $40,000-$60,000, $1,165.50 + 4.44%; $60,000 and over, $2,053.50 + 4.82%. Residents with taxable income under $100,000 must use the 2025 Tax Table (booklet p.36), which follows the same rates in small income bands. Computation (IT-140): federal AGI (line 1), plus increasing and minus decreasing Schedule M modifications, gives WV AGI. Subtract the Low-Income Earned Income Exclusion and exemptions ($2,000 each; $500 if zero exemptions, e.g. claimed as a dependent) to get WV taxable income. West Virginia has no standard deduction. Federal income tax is not deductible. Tips and overtime: no Schedule M modification for them appears in the 2025 booklet, and the federal deductions are below AGI, so they do not affect West Virginia. A 2026-session conformity bill was not examined for retroactivity to 2025. HB 2026 of the 2025 Regular Session is the Budget Bill (WV Legislature bill status: 'SUMMARY: Budget Bill', effective from passage April 11, 2025). It did not change 2025 rates, and the official 2025 schedule shows 2.22%-4.82%. SB 392 (2026) cut rates 5% to 2.11%-4.58% for tax year 2026 only (WV Tax Division page). The LIEIE (FAGI <= $10,000) and Family Tax Credit (zero above modified FAGI $18,350 for one person) do not apply at wages of $20k or more. Illustrative 2025 tax (schedule): $20k = TI $18,000, $458.80; $40k = $1,098.90; $80k = $2,921.10; $120k = $4,849.10. Local: West Virginia has no local income tax. Tax Foundation footnote (a) lists WV among states where some jurisdictions levy payroll or flat-rate wage taxes; from background knowledge (not verified in this pass), these are flat per-worker municipal 'city service' or user fees in some cities, not percentage wage taxes. Amounts were not verified, so the value is set to 0. No discrepancies with Tax Foundation (TF: 2.22%-4.82%, $2,000 exemption).

phaseouts.applies_to: Low-Income Earned Income Exclusion (IT-140 line 5; subtraction from WV AGI)
phaseouts.formula: If federal AGI <= $10,000 (single): exclusion = min(federal AGI, earned income, $10,000); otherwise 0. Not applicable at wages of $20k or more.

phaseouts.applies_to: Family Tax Credit (nonrefundable, a percentage of IT-140 line 8 tax). Family size 1 is a single filer claiming 1 exemption.
phaseouts.formula: pct = 100% if modified FAGI <= $15,650, falling 10 points per $300 ($15,650-$15,950 = 90% ... $18,050-$18,350 = 10%), and 0% above $18,350. Not applicable at wages of $20k or more.

West Virginia.changes_vs_2024: Rates cut about 6% for 2025 with the brackets unchanged. 2024 Rate Schedule I was 2.36%/3.15%/3.54%/4.72%/5.12%; 2025 is 2.22%/2.96%/3.33%/4.44%/4.82%. Per secondary sources (EY Tax News 2024-2154; news coverage), this reflects the 4% revenue-trigger reduction plus the 2% SB 2033 cut (2024 2nd Ext. Sess.), both effective 1/1/2025. The $2,000 exemption is unchanged; the 2024 figure was not separately re-checked. Illustrative at $40k wages (TI $38,000): 2024 $1,168.70 ($708.50 + 3.54% x $13,000) vs 2025 $1,098.90 (-$69.80).

Wisconsin.notes: Brackets: Wis. Stat. 71.06(1r) as amended by 2025 Act 15 reads 3.50% on $0-$14,680; 4.40% on $14,680-$50,480; 5.30% on $50,480-$323,290; 7.65% above. This is confirmed by the 2025 Form 1 instructions Tax Computation Worksheet (single, TI $100,000-$323,290: 5.3% x TI - $586.44, which implies 0.009 x (14,680 + 50,480) = 586.44; above $323,290: 7.65% x TI - $8,183.76) and by 2025 Tax Table rows (e.g., TI $41,300-$41,400 shows tax $1,687 = 4.4% bracket). Filers with TI < $100,000 must use the Tax Table ($100 rows, tax at row midpoint). Standard deduction: sliding scale (see phaseouts), max $13,560, reduced 12% per dollar of Wisconsin income over $19,549, zero at $132,549. The formula is derived from and checked against the official 2025 Standard Deduction Table at $20,250, $40,250, $80,250 and $120,250 midpoints. Value used at ~$40k: $11,076 (table row $40,000-$40,500); exact formula at $40,000 = $11,106. Values: $20k 13,476 (table) / 13,506 (formula); $80k 6,276 / 6,306; $120k 1,476 / 1,506. Personal exemption: $700 deduction (Form 1 line 10a). Starts from federal AGI (Form 1 line 1). Wisconsin uses the IRC as of 12/31/2022 with exceptions. The federal tips/overtime deductions are below-AGI and Wisconsin has no 2025 subtraction for them (none listed in 'New in 2025'), so they do not reduce Wisconsin tax. No local income taxes. Excluded credits: school property tax credit (renters and owners, up to $300), homestead credit (low income), itemized deduction credit, and Wisconsin EITC (requires qualifying children). Check values (wages = WI income, table method): $40k: TI = 40,000 - 11,076 - 700 = 28,224, tax about $1,111 (table). DISCREPANCIES WITH TAX FOUNDATION: TF shows the second bracket ending at $29,370 (indexed pre-Act-15 law as of 1/1/2025); 2025 law extends 4.4% to $50,480. TF's $14,680 and $323,290 thresholds, $13,560 standard deduction, $19,549/$132,549 phase-out (footnote ii) and $700 exemption match 2025.

phaseouts.applies_to: standard_deduction
phaseouts.formula: Single sliding-scale standard deduction = max(0, 13560 - 0.12 * max(0, WI_income - 19549)), where WI_income = Form 1 line 7 (federal AGI +/- Wisconsin modifications; about equal to wages for a simple wage earner). Phases to zero at $132,549. The official 2025 Standard Deduction Table (used by filers) evaluates this at the midpoint of $500 income rows, so table values run about $30 below the exact formula at row starts.

Wisconsin.changes_vs_2024: Material. 2025 Wis. Act 15 created Wis. Stat. 71.06(1r) for taxable years beginning after 12/31/2024: the 4.4% bracket now runs to $50,480 (single), up from $29,370 under the indexed pre-Act-15 law. 2024 single brackets: 3.5% to $14,320; 4.4% to $28,640; 5.3% to $315,310; 7.65% above (2024 Tax Computation Worksheet subtraction $386.64 and top threshold $315,310). Standard deduction maximum rose from $13,230 (2024) to $13,560 (2025), with the 12% phase-out start moving from about $19,070 (my derivation from the 2024 table) to $19,549. Effect: about $0.009 x (taxable income above $29,370, capped at $21,110), i.e. up to $190 saved for single filers with TI above $50,480 versus pre-Act law, plus indexing gains versus 2024. Exemption unchanged at $700.

Wyoming.notes: No individual or corporate income tax. No local income taxes. starts_from is a placeholder.

District of Columbia.notes: Source: 2025 D-40 booklet (OTR). Rate table, Calculation I, single: <= $10,000 4%; $10,000-40,000 $400 + 6%; $40,000-60,000 $2,200 + 6.5%; $60,000-250,000 $3,500 + 8.5%; $250,000-500,000 $19,650 + 9.25%; $500,000-1M $42,775 + 9.75%; > $1M $91,525 + 10.75%. The base amounts equal the cumulative marginal tax. STANDARD DEDUCTION: in Nov 2025 the D.C. Council decoupled from OBBBA's higher federal basic standard deduction (P.L. 119-21, $15,750). DC's own 2025 basic standard deduction is $15,000 single/dependent/MFS ($22,500 HOH), plus an additional $2,000 for a single filer who is 65+ or blind. DC also does not allow the federal Schedule 1-A deductions (tips, overtime, car loan interest, senior deduction). No personal exemption. Income starts from federal AGI, plus DC additions and minus subtractions (Schedule I), to give DC AGI. Federal tax is not deductible. DC disallows the deduction for state and local income taxes when itemizing. New 2025 DC filing threshold: gross income >= $15,000 (single), even if no federal return is required. Examples (wages only): $20k: TI 5,000, $200. $40k: TI 25,000, $1,300. $80k: TI 65,000, $3,925. $120k: TI 105,000, $7,325. Not included: DC EITC (100% of federal for 2025) and the Schedule H homeowner/renter property tax credit (refundable, up to $1,425, FAGI <= $66,000 for claimants under 70), which is relevant to many renters below $66k. LOCAL: none beyond DC itself. Tax Foundation 2025 matches: its $15,000 equals DC's own decoupled amount, not the OBBBA $15,750.
District of Columbia.changes_vs_2024: Standard deduction rose from $14,600 (2024, equal to federal; 2024 D-40 booklet) to $15,000 (2025, DC-defined). That is -$24 tax at the 6% bracket, -$26 at 6.5% and -$34 at 8.5%. Rates are unchanged since TY2022. Not included but changed: DC EITC rose to 100% of federal; the DC child tax credit was repealed for 2025 (n/a here); the Schedule H property tax credit maximum rose to $1,425 with a $66,000 FAGI limit (under 70).
